chapters.title: The Ballot from the Cell
beats: In the shadow of the First World War, a bitter ideological war erupted within the United States, pitting the federal government against its own citizens over the limits of free speech and economic justice.
At the height of this national crisis, a charismatic political leader mounted a historic presidential campaign while locked inside a federal penitentiary.
This unprecedented challenge to the two-party system rallied nearly a million voters, pitting the power of the state against a rising tide of early American democratic socialism.
How did an imprisoned labor organizer manage to capture the imagination of the American electorate, and what did his defiance cost the nation's political establishment?
chapters.hook: Before he was a prisoner, he was the master of the nation's rails.

chapters.title: The Players on the Stage
beats: The drama of early American socialism centers on Eugene Victor Debs, a passionate labor organizer from Terre Haute, Indiana, who sought to unite the working class against corporate greed through peaceful electoral politics.
Opposing his vision of industrial democracy was President Grover Cleveland, a conservative Democrat who believed the federal government must use military force to protect commerce and break strikes.
Within the labor movement itself, Debs faced internal opposition from Bill Haywood, a radical unionist who rejected political compromise and demanded direct action to overthrow capitalism.
As global war approached, President Woodrow Wilson emerged as Debs's most formidable adversary, viewing any opposition to the military draft as a treasonous threat to national survival.
Years later, President Warren G. Harding would inherit the political fallout of this struggle, tasked with deciding whether to keep the aging socialist leader locked away or show clemency.
The crucial battleground of this story was Chicago, Illinois, the nation's industrial heartland where massive rail yards and factories served as the ultimate test of labor's collective power.

chapters.title: The Fireman's Rise
beats: Eugene Victor Debs is born in Terre Haute, Indiana in November 1855, and is pressed into service as a night railroad fireman in December 1871.
By February 1875, Debs joins the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, adopting the union motto "Benevolence, Sobriety, and Industry" as his guiding light.
Debs is elected as a Democrat to the Indiana General Assembly in 1884, but soon realizes that legislative politics under the two major parties fails to protect working people.
Seeking stronger solidarity, Debs steps down from his union post in February 1893 to organize the American Railway Union, embracing "the need to reorganize across craft lines."
In the summer of 1894, the nationwide Pullman Strike erupts in Chicago, Illinois, prompting President Grover Cleveland to send federal troops to crush the strike.
The New York Times editorializes that Debs is "a lawbreaker at large, an enemy of the human race," leading to his arrest and a six months prison sentence.

While in prison, a visitor delivers a message that changes him forever, prompting Debs to write that he "came to Woodstock, as if a providential instrument, and delivered the first impassioned message of Socialism I had ever heard."
chapters.hook: But as Debs embraced the ballot box, a more radical voice rose to challenge his peaceful path.

chapters.title: The Split in the Ranks
beats: Following his release, Debs helps establish the Social Democratic Party of America in June 1898 to pursue power through the ballot box.
Debs runs for president in 1900, earning 0.6 percent of the vote, and runs again in 1904, increasing his share to 3.0 percent.
In June 1905, Debs joins Bill Haywood in Chicago, Illinois to found the Industrial Workers of the World, aiming to build one giant union.
Haywood declares to the convention, "We are here to confederate the workers of this country into a working-class movement that shall have for its purpose the emancipation of the working class."

However, ideological rifts quickly emerge as Haywood mocks moderate political action, calling parliamentary socialists "step-at-a-time people whose every step is just a little shorter than the preceding step."
Haywood argues it is better to "elect the superintendent of some branch of industry, than to elect some congressman to the United States Congress."
Moderate socialist leaders like Morris Hillquit condemn Haywood's syndicalist ideas as "purely anarchistic," leading to a bitter split.
Despite the internal chaos, Debs achieves his peak electoral strength in the 1912 presidential election, winning 6.0 percent of the popular vote.

chapters.title: The Canton Speech
beats: As World War I rages in Europe, President Woodrow Wilson asks Congress in December 1915 for strict legislation to restrict espionage and domestic interference.
Congress passes the Espionage Act of 1917, which is soon extended by the passage of the Sedition Act of 1918 to criminalize anti-war speech.
On June 16, 1918, Eugene Victor Debs climbs onto a stage in Canton, Ohio, fully aware of the federal agents watching him from the crowd.
Debs delivers a passionate, public speech urging resistance to the military draft, directly challenging the authority of the federal government.
For Woodrow Wilson, this public defiance during a national crisis is an intolerable threat that requires immediate and decisive federal action.

chapters.title: Conviction and Campaign
beats: On June 30, 1918, Debs is arrested and charged with ten counts of sedition for his anti-draft speech in Canton, Ohio.
In September 1918, a federal judge sentences Debs to ten years in prison and disenfranchises him for life, a sentence he begins serving in April 1919.
Woodrow Wilson fiercely opposes any clemency for the socialist leader, branding Debs a "traitor to his country" and stating, "I doubt the wisdom and public effect of such an action."
Despite being locked behind bars in Atlanta, Georgia, the Socialist Party nominates Debs as their presidential candidate for the fifth time in 1920.
Campaigning from his prison cell as Convict No. 9653, Debs champions the working class, earning the nickname "the Lincoln of Labor."
In the 1920 election, Debs wins 914,191 votes, representing 3.4 percent of the popular vote, proving his enduring political appeal.
In March 1921, Debs travels to Washington, D.C. to meet with President Warren G. Harding's Attorney General, Harry Daugherty, to discuss his confinement.
Recognizing that the war is over, President Warren G. Harding commutes Debs's sentence to time served on December 23, 1921, releasing him on Christmas Day.

chapters.title: The Final Embers
beats: Following his release, Debs continues to advocate for working-class solidarity, though his health is permanently shattered by his years in prison.

In 1924, European supporters like Karl H. Wiik nominate Debs for the Nobel Peace Prize, noting that "Debs started to work actively for peace during World War I, mainly because he considered the war to be in the interest of capitalism."
On October 20, 1926, Eugene Victor Debs dies of heart failure at the age of 70 in Elmhurst, Illinois, leaving behind a legacy of radical dissent.

Decades later, his political vision continues to inspire reformers; in 1979, future senator Bernie Sanders produces a documentary praising Debs as "probably the most effective and popular leader that the American working class has ever had."
In 1966, Debs's home in Terre Haute, Indiana is officially designated a National Historic Landmark to preserve his memory.
Finally, in 1990, the American labor movement cements his place in history with his formal induction into the Labor Hall of Fame.
